...good people are found within the church, even those who are in heresies but in a life of good; and, outside the church, all who are in good. But with these, <term>falsities</term> <note>In this context, "falsities" refers to incorrect religious doctrines or intellectual mistakes rather than intentional lies.</note> do not condemn them, unless they are the kind of falsities that are opposed to good and destroy the very life of good. 

But the falsities which are not opposed to good are indeed in themselves falsities; yet, relative to the **good of life** to which they are not opposed, they almost lose the quality of falsity. This happens through their application to good. For such falsities can be applied to good, just as they can be applied to evil. If they are applied to good, they become mild; but if to evil, they become hard. Indeed, falsities can be applied to good just as easily as truths can be applied to evil; for all truths, whatever they may be, are **falsified** through applications to evil. 

Take as an example the doctrine that **faith alone saves.** <note>original: "fidem solam". This refers to the theological debate over whether belief alone, without good deeds, is sufficient for salvation.</note> In itself, this is a falsity—especially with those who are evil, who use it to shut out the good of <term>charity</term> <note>Charity here refers to the active practice of love and kindness toward others.</note> as if it contributed nothing at all to salvation. But this falsity becomes **mild** with those who are in the good of life. They apply it to good by saying that faith alone saves, but that it is not truly "faith" unless it is accompanied by its "fruit"—consequently, only where good is present. So it is in all other cases.

**[2]** In what now follows, all those are treated of who had been in falsities from evil, and in evil from falsities, and who were cast into hell when the Lord came into the world. For there are very many kinds of evil, and consequently also many kinds of falsity, because every kind of evil has its own falsity joined to it. For falsity is produced from evil and is simply **evil in its form**, just as the <term>understanding</term> in a person is the form of their <term>will</term>. <note>The author uses a psychological model where the "Will" is the source of desire/intent, and the "Understanding" is the faculty that gives those desires shape, thought, and language.</note> This is because the will reveals itself in the light of the understanding; it shapes and forms itself there, presenting itself through images, then through ideas, and finally through words. 

These things have been said so that it may be known that there are many kinds of evil and of the resulting falsity. These were first described under the name of "**the Egyptians**"; and now in these verses under the name of "**the inhabitants of Philistia**," "**the leaders of Edom**," "**the mighty ones of Moab**," and "**the inhabitants of Canaan**." **8313.** *Pain hath laid hold of the inhabitants of Philistia.* That this signifies despair of enlarging their dominion on the part of those who are in **faith separate from good** <note>This refers to the theological position that belief alone is sufficient for salvation, without the need for a life of good deeds or charity.</note>, is evident from the meaning of “pain,” as being despair on account of their being no longer able to enlarge their dominion (discussed further below); and from the meaning of “the inhabitants of Philistia,” as being those who are in **faith alone** separate from the **good of charity** <note>original: "bono caritatis". * that salvation is granted by mercy regardless of how the person has lived; 
* that through faith all sins and evils are washed away; 
* and that thus the person marches along **justified** <note>To be "justified" here means to be made righteous or acceptable in the eyes of God.</note>; 
* also that salvation can be effected in a moment, even in the final hour of death, through the trust of faith; 
* consequently, that it is not the affection of **celestial love** <note>A deep, heavenly love for God and others that characterizes the state of heaven.</note> that makes heaven within a person. 

These are the “Philistines,” and they were called “the uncircumcised” by reason of the evils of the love of self and of the world, in which their life resides. [2] The reason “pain” here denotes despair is because the word implies the utmost pain, such as that of women in labor. Moreover, in the **original tongue** <note>original: "lingua originali". This refers to the Hebrew language in which the Old Testament was written.</note> the word signifies such pain. Despair or the most extreme pain is also described in the **Word** <note>The "Word" refers to the Holy Scriptures or the Bible.</note> by “the pain of a woman in labor,” as in these passages:

> The kings gathered themselves together, terror seized them, pain as of a woman in travail (Psalm 48:4, 6).

### [N. 8313] CHAPTER XV. VERSES 14-16

From this, it is clear that “pain” here signifies despair due to the injury of what is good.

[4] That “pain has laid hold of the inhabitants of Philistia” signifies despair, or the loss of hope in expanding their power. ### CHAPTER XV. VERSES 14-16

**8314.** [continued] ...predicated of truth. [2] It should be known that in the Word <note>The "Word" refers to the Sacred Scriptures or the Bible.</note> there are specific words belonging to the class of **spiritual things**, and others belonging to the class of **celestial things**. That is to say, some terms express concepts related to **truth** or **faith**, while others express concepts related to **goodness** or **love**. There are also words used for both. 

One who understands these distinctions can recognize, at first glance or upon reading the Word—especially in its original language—where the internal meaning is dealing with matters of truth or matters of goodness. This is the case with the meanings of "princes" and "chiefs." "Princes" signify primary or foundational things and are associated with the truths of faith; however, "chiefs" <note>original: *duces*, often translated as "dukes" or "leaders"</note> signify principal or essential things and are associated with the good of love. In the opposite sense, "princes" refer to the falsehoods of faith, and "chiefs" to the evils of love. 

[3] This is why those who ruled in Edom were called "chiefs" (*Genesis* 36:15-21, 29, 30, 40-43). The reason is that "Edom" symbolized the good of celestial love, and in its opposite sense, the evil of self-love. But among the sons of Ishmael, those who presided over the others were not called "chiefs," but "princes" (*Genesis* 25:16), because "Ishmael" symbolized those who are focused on truth (see section numbers 3263, 3268, 4747). 

For this same reason, those who presided over Israel were called "princes" (*Numbers* 7:2, 10, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 54), for Israel represented those who possess the truth and goodness of faith. However, those who presided over Judah were called "chiefs," because Judah represented those who are in the good of love, as seen in the book of *Zechariah*:

->Let him be as a chief in Judah (9:7).<-
->The chiefs of Judah shall say in their heart, I will confirm to me the inhabitants of Jerusalem in Jehovah Zebaoth <note>The Hebrew title "Lord of Hosts."</note> their God; in that day I will make the chiefs of Judah like a furnace of fire in pieces of wood (12:5, 6).<-

This is evident from the meaning of "mighty ones" as things that rule and prevail, and from the representation of Moab as those who possess <term>natural good</term> <note>A kind of kindness or morality based on personality or upbringing rather than spiritual principles.</note> but allow themselves to be easily led astray (see section number 2468). Consequently, they live a life of falsity; for those who possess natural good, but not the goodness that comes from...

# NUMBER 8318] CHAPTER XV. VERSES 14–16

...continually desire to <term>domineer</term> <note>to exercise absolute control or mastery over others</note>, but when terror falls upon them on account of a victorious enemy, then the hope of domineering falls. 

[2] Be it known that <term>evils</term> <note>spiritually destructive behaviors or intentions</note> arise from two distinct origins: namely, from the **love of self**, and from the **love of the world**. They who are in evils from the **love of self** love themselves only, and despise all others except those who act as one with them. In loving those people, they do not actually love them, but rather themselves, because they see their own reflection in them. 

The evils from this origin are the worst of all; for they who are in them not only despise everyone else in comparison with themselves, but also pursue others with insults and bear hatred toward them for the slightest reason, even breathing their destruction. In this way, revenge and cruelty become the delight of their life. Those who are in the evil of this love are in a deep place in <term>hell</term> <note>a spiritual state of total self-absorption and misery</note> according to the intensity and amount of this love.

[3] But they who are in evil from the **love of the world** also hold their neighbor in slight estimation, and value others solely by reason of their wealth—thus they value their riches, not the person. These people desire to possess everything that belongs to their neighbor, and when they are in this <term>cupidity</term> <note>an intense, selfish greed for gain</note>, they are entirely devoid of all charity and mercy; for depriving their neighbor of his goods is the delight of their life. This is especially true of those who are <term>sordidly avaricious</term> <note>miserly or greedy for money for its own sake rather than for its useful purpose</note>, that is, who love gold and silver for the sake of gold and silver, but not for the sake of any use that comes from them. 

Those in whom the evil of this love rules are also in the hells, but not in hells as deep as those who are in the evil of the love of self. Besides these two origins of evil there is also a third, which is to do evil from the principles of a **false religion**; but this evil is only of a bad character in those who are also in the love of self and of the world. It is not so in those who are in love toward their neighbor and toward their God; for in their case, the <term>end</term> <note>the ultimate purpose or intention behind an action</note> is good, and the end qualifies everything else (see number 8311).

# EXODUS [NO. 8321]

8321. ***Until Thy people shall pass over.*** That this signifies that thus without danger of <term>infestation</term> <note>spiritual harassment or the "injection" of false thoughts and evil desires by malevolent spirits</note> all shall be saved who are capable of receiving the truth of good and the good of truth, is evident from the signification of "passing over," as being to be saved without danger of infestation; for when they who are in <term>falsities</term> <note>spiritual errors or distorted beliefs</note> from evil, and have infested others, are cast into <term>hell</term> <note>a spiritual state of total self-absorption and misery</note>, and are removed, then there are none who obstruct by injecting falsities and evils, and who thus prevent the reception of good and truth from the <term>Lord</term> <note>referring to the Divine</note>. This is what is here signified by "passing over." 

For so long as the evil were not cast into hell, scarcely any could "pass over," that is, be saved; for the evil then continually excited evils and falsities with those who were coming into the other life, and thus withheld them from good and truth. In order therefore that those who were in good and truth might be liberated from such infesters, the Lord came into the world; and when He was in the world, then by means of continual <term>temptations</term> <note>internal spiritual conflicts or trials</note> admitted into Himself, and by means of continual victories therein, He subjugated all such spirits, and afterward by His presence caused them to be cast into hell, where being taken possession of by their own evils and falsities, they might be kept bound to eternity. 

[2] By "people" are here meant those who are in the capacity of receiving the truth of good and the good of truth, for "people" in general signifies those who are in the truth and good of faith (see references n. 1259, 1260, 3295, 3581, 4619); here, it signifies Israel, that is, those who are of the <term>spiritual church</term> <note>a community of believers defined by their commitment to truth and the life of charity, rather than just ritual</note>, or what is the same, who are in the truth of good and the good of truth (n. 7957, 8234). 

It is said "in the capacity of receiving the truth of good and the good of truth," because no others are in this capacity than those who have lived a life of **charity**. This life gives this capacity. Hugely do those err who believe that **faith without charity** can confer this quality; for faith without charity is hard and resistant, and rejects all the <term>influx</term> <note>the constant flow of life, love, and wisdom</note> from the Lord; but charity with faith is yielding and gentle and receives the influx. From this it is that charity gives this capacity, but not faith without charity; and as charity gives this capacity, it is this also which saves; for they who are saved are not saved through charity from themselves, but through charity from the Lord, consequently through the capacity of receiving it.

<summary>This entry explains that "passing over" symbolizes salvation free from the harassment of evil spirits, made possible by the Lord's victory over hell. It emphasizes that salvation depends on "charity" (active love), which makes a person receptive to Divine influence, whereas faith alone remains resistant.</summary>

# EXODUS [No. 8324]

...those who were in the good of truth and in the truth of good passed safely through the region of that hell.

**8325.** ***Thou shalt bring them in.*** That this signifies elevation, is evident from the meaning of "bringing in," when it refers to heaven, as being elevation. It is called "elevation" because, to the outward sight of spirits, heaven is on high; however, to the inner sight—such as that of the angels—heaven is within. This is because everything internal in the afterlife is represented as being above, and everything external as being below; consequently, heaven appears above and hell beneath (see references 2148, 3084, 4599, 5146). In short, states of truth and of good (and in the opposite sense, states of falsity and of evil) are represented in the afterlife through heights and depths—that is, through distances and places (see references 2625, 2837, 3356, 3387, 4321, 4882, 5605, 7381). 

[2] From this experience alone, one can see how difficult it is for the <term>natural man</term> <note>The "natural man" refers to the part of the human mind that focuses only on the physical world and sensory information, often struggling to grasp abstract spiritual concepts.</note> to understand spiritual things, and consequently the things of heaven. What natural man can comprehend that there are no spaces or times in heaven, but instead "states"? Specifically, there are states of good (or states of *being* <note>original: "esse"</note>) instead of space; and states of truth (or states of *becoming* <note>original: "existere"</note>) instead of time. Will not the merely natural man believe that there is absolute emptiness and nothingness where there is no time and space? 

From this it is clear that if the natural man decides that nothing is to be believed except what he can physically grasp, he then falls into enormous errors. As it is with space and time, so it is with many other things. For example, the natural man inevitably falls into <term>phantasy</term> <note>In this context, a "phantasy" is a delusional or false mental image that lacks spiritual reality.</note> regarding the Divine when he thinks from the perspective of time about what God was doing before the creation of the world—that is, what the Divine had done from eternity until then. He cannot be untangled from this knot until the ideas of time and space are removed. When the angels think about this eternity, they never think about it in terms of time, but in terms of "state." 

[3] In the afterlife, there appear two statues, partly of flesh and partly of stone, placed at the boundary of the created universe, in front toward the left. It is said of them that they "swallow" those who try to think about what the Divine was doing from eternity until the world was created <note>This striking image serves as a symbolic warning against applying finite, physical logic—like the passage of time—to the infinite nature of God.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the spiritual commentary on Exodus 15:17. # CHAPTER XV. VERSES 17–19

This "swallowing up" represents how a person, because they cannot think except through the lenses of space and time, cannot free themselves from these limitations by their own power. However, they can do so through the Divine. This is achieved either by breaking up these limited patterns of thought or by removing the concepts of time entirely.

**8326.** *And plant them.* This symbolizes <term>regeneration</term> <note>Regeneration refers to the spiritual process of being "reborn" or reformed by God, moving from a self-centered life to one led by love and faith.</note> occurring continually. This is evident from the meaning of "planting" as being regenerated, for the process of spiritual rebirth is very similar to planting. When a tree is planted, it grows into branches, leaves, and fruits; from the seeds of those fruits, new trees grow, and the cycle continues. Human regeneration works the same way. For this reason, in the Word <note>In this context, "the Word" refers to the inner, symbolic meaning of the Bible.</note>, a person is often compared to a tree, and a reborn person to a garden or paradise. In this comparison, the truths of faith are like leaves, the good deeds of charity are like fruits, and the seeds—from which new trees grow—are the truths that spring from a good heart (or, in other words, faith that springs from love). This is described as "continual" regeneration because, while the process begins in this world, it never stops. It is perfected throughout this life and into the next life for all eternity; yet, it can never reach such a state of perfection that it could be compared to the Divine.

**8327.** *In the mountain of Thine inheritance.* This signifies heaven, specifically where the good of charity exists. This is clear because a "mountain" symbolizes the <term>good of love</term> <note>In the symbolic language of Scripture, "good of love" refers to the quality of a life motivated by selfless love for God and others.</note> (see numbers 795, 796, 2722, 4210, 6435), and "inheritance" refers to the life of another—in this case, the life of the Lord. Thus, it refers to a life of goodness and truth that comes from the Lord. Those who live this life are called "heirs of the kingdom" and "children" (numbers 2658, 2851, 3672, 7212). Because these concepts are linked to the "mountain of inheritance," it also signifies heaven; for heaven is defined by the good of love, and it serves as an inheritance for those who belong to the Lord.

It is also evident from the meaning of "the habitation of the Lord" <note>original: "Jehovah"</note>, or "the place for You to dwell in," as being wherever the Lord is present.

## Section 8344

**Verses 22–26.** *And Moses made Israel set out from the Sea of Reeds <note>original: "mare Suph"; commonly known as the Red Sea.</note>, and they went out to the wilderness of Shur; and they went three days in the wilderness, and found no waters. And they came to Bitterness <note>original: "Marah", which literally means bitterness in Hebrew.</note>, and they could not drink the waters for bitterness, because they were bitter; therefore he called the name thereof Bitterness. And the people murmured against Moses, saying, What shall we drink? And he cried unto the Lord <note>original: "Jehovah". The author identifies the Jehovah of the Old Testament with the Lord Jesus Christ.</note>, and the Lord showed him a piece of wood, and he cast it to the waters, and the waters were made sweet. There He set for him a statute and a judgment, and there He tempted him. And He said, If hearing thou wilt hear the voice of the Lord thy God, and wilt do what is right in His eyes, and wilt hearken to His commandments, and wilt keep all His statutes, all the disease that I have put on the Egyptians, I will not put upon thee, because I am the Lord thy healer.*

**“And Moses made Israel set out from the Sea of Reeds,”** signifies what follows in the orderly progression of <term>Divine truth</term> <note>Divine Truth: The spiritual laws and light emanating from God that guide the human mind.</note> after they had passed through a region of hell;

**“and they went out to the wilderness of Shur,”** signifies the state of <term>temptation</term> <note>Temptation: In this context, a spiritual trial or inner struggle where one’s faith and character are tested.</note> into which they were next brought;

**“and they went three days in the wilderness, and found no waters,”** signifies that truths failed, and eventually disappeared entirely;

**“and they came to Bitterness,”** signifies a state of temptation;

**“and they could not drink the waters for bitterness, because they were bitter,”** signifies that truths appeared to them undelightful, because they lacked the <term>affection of good</term> <note>Affection of good: A heartfelt love for doing what is right and kind; without this love, even correct information can feel cold or "bitter."</note>;

**“therefore he called the name thereof Bitterness,”** signifies the state and specific quality of this temptation;

**“and the people murmured against Moses,”** signifies the grief or distress arising from the bitterness of the temptation;

**“saying, What shall we drink?”** signifies that they could not endure truths, because they were unpleasant when not accompanied by a love for them;

**“and he cried unto the Lord,”** signifies a prayer of supplication to the Lord arising from grief;

**“and the Lord showed him a piece of wood,”** signifies that the Lord inspired a sense of good <note>In the author's symbolic system, "wood" often represents the "good of life" or practical kindness.</note>;

**“and he cast it into the waters,”** signifies that He combined this goodness with the truths they possessed;

**“and the waters were made sweet,”** signifies that as a result, the truths became delightful;

**“there He set for him a statute and a judgment,”** signifies the laws of order that were then revealed;

**“and there He tempted him,”** signifies that this refers to the nature of spiritual trials in general;

**“and He said,”** signifies instruction;

The transformation of the bitter water into sweet represents how the Lord makes spiritual life delightful through the inspiration of love.</summary>

"Against Moses," because it was against the Divine, for by Moses is represented **Divine truth** (see n. 6723, 6752, 6771, 6827, 7010, 7014, 7089, 7382). 

[2] As regards the <term>temptations</term> <note>In this theology, "temptations" are not just urges to do wrong, but internal spiritual struggles or "growing pains" where a person's old habits of thought and will are challenged by new spiritual ideals.</note> which those underwent who were of the <term>spiritual church</term> <note>The "spiritual church" refers to people who are led toward what is good by first learning truths and principles, rather than by direct intuitive love.</note>, and which those will undergo who will be of this church, be it known that faith cannot possibly be implanted in those who are of the spiritual church except through temptations; the same is true of charity. # N. 8352] CHAPTER XV. VERS. 22-26

The life of heaven now seems undelightful to them, insomuch that they can scarcely endure them. [2] The <term>merely natural man</term> <note>The "natural man" refers to someone who lives primarily for the physical world and sensory experiences, without a developed sense of spiritual purpose.</note> would not believe that such a thing could cause any grief, for he thinks, "What is it to me whether truths are delightful or not? If they are undelightful let them be rejected." 

But the <term>spiritual man</term> <note>The "spiritual man" is one whose inner mind has been opened to understand and love divine truths.</note> has very different sentiments. It is the delight of his life to be instructed in truths, and to be enlightened in such things as belong to his soul, thus to his spiritual life; and therefore when these fail, his spiritual life labors and suffers, and grief and anxiety ensue. The reason is that the <term>affection of good</term> <note>In this context, "affection" refers to a deep, driving love or desire. An "affection of good" is a heartfelt yearning to do what is right.</note> is continually flowing in through the <term>internal man</term> from the Lord, and calling forth the accordant things in the <term>external man</term> which had previously caused the delight of the affection of truth; and when these things are assaulted by the evils of the love of self and of the world, which the man had also previously perceived as delightful, there arises a conflict of delights or of affections, from which springs anxiety, and from this grief and complaint. 

[3] It shall be briefly told how the case is with the <term>temptation</term> <note>Here, "temptation" is an internal struggle where a person's old selfish habits clash with their new spiritual ideals.</note> that arises through a failing of truth. The nourishment of the spiritual life is good and truth, as the nourishment of the natural life is food and drink. If good fails, it is as if food fails; and if truth fails, it is as if drink fails. The consequent grief is circumstanced like the grief from hunger and thirst. 

This comparison is from <term>correspondence</term> <note>Correspondence is the symbolic relationship between the physical world and the spiritual world. For example, physical water "corresponds" to spiritual truth because both provide essential refreshment and cleansing.</note>, for food corresponds to good, and drink to truth; and as there is a correspondence, food and drink also nourish the body better and more suitably when a man at dinner or at breakfast is at the same time in the delight of conversation with others about such things as he loves, than when he sits at table alone without company. When a man is in this state, the vessels in him that receive the food are constricted; but when he is in the first mentioned state, they are open. 

Such things are effected by the correspondence of spiritual food and natural food. It is said "the delight of conversation with others about such things as he loves," because everything of this kind has relation to **good** and **truth**; for there is nothing in the world which has not relation to both. What a man loves, has relation to the **good** with him; and what instructs him about good, and thus conjoins itself with it, has relation to the **truth**.

**8353.** ***And he cried unto Jehovah.*** This signifies a heartfelt plea to the Lord arising from sorrow. This is clear from the meaning of "crying" as an act of imploration <note>original: "imploratio"</note> and internal mourning; consequently, it also refers to a prayer or supplication born from grief. **8354.** ***And Jehovah showed him a piece of wood.*** This signifies that the Lord inspired a sense of <term>good</term> <note>In this context, "good" (Latin: *bonum*) refers to the quality of love, kindness, and charity that motivates a person's actions.</note>. This is shown by the meaning of "showing"—when performed by Jehovah (the Lord)—as giving a person perception. Since this perception is given through <term>influx</term> <note>Influx is the spiritual process where life and thought flow from the divine into the human mind.</note>, it denotes inspiration. It is also shown by the meaning of "wood" as representing goodness (n. 643, 2784, 2812, 3720).

**8355.** ***And he cast it into the waters.*** This signifies the way the Lord affected truths with this goodness. This is clear from the meaning of "casting wood into the waters": since "wood" represents goodness and "waters" represent <term>truths</term> <note>Here, "truths" (Latin: *vera*) refer to the facts of faith and spiritual principles a person learns.</note>, the act represents influencing those truths with a sense of love or goodness. (That "wood" means good and "waters" mean truths has been established in previous sections.)

**8356.** ***And the waters were made sweet.*** This signifies that, as a result, these spiritual truths became delightful. This is evident from the meaning of "sweet" as something that brings joy or delight; in a spiritual sense, "sweetness" refers to the sweetness of life, which is the same as delight. This is also shown by the meaning of "waters" as truths.

The situation is as follows: The reason a person is moved by a truth is because of the "good" within it. Goodness and truth are joined together like a marriage; consequently, one loves the other as a husband or wife loves their spouse. Because of this, the union of goodness and truth is often compared in the Bible to a "marriage," and the truths and goods born from this union are called "sons and daughters."

From this, we can see that the delight we feel when we are affected by a truth comes from no other source than goodness itself. This is also proven by experience: those who live a good life—meaning those who love God and their neighbor—also love the truths of faith. Therefore, as long as goodness flows in from the Lord and is accepted, truth appears delightful. However, as soon as that goodness stops flowing—that is, as soon as evil begins to take over and blocks the flow of goodness—a person immediately feels a lack of...

In what precedes, the first temptation in the wilderness was treated of; in what follows, instruction how they must live in order that they may not yield in temptations is treated of.

**8359.** ***And He said.*** That this signifies instruction, is evident from the signification of "saying," when by <term>Jehovah</term> <note>The author identifies "Jehovah" in the Old Testament as the Lord (Jesus Christ) acting in His divine capacity.</note> concerning the truth of order in respect to temptations, as being instruction (see also n. 6879, 6881, 6883, 6891, 7186, 7267, 7304, 7380, 7517, 8127).

**8361.** ***And wilt do what is right in His eyes.*** That this signifies a life according to them, is evident from the signification of "doing what is right," as being to live according to the dictations of truth.

When the temptation is ended, communication with heaven is opened, which had previously been partly closed, consequently enlightenment and affection, and consequently pleasantness and delight; for then the angels with whom communication is given, flow in by means of truth, and by means of good. Enlightenment by means of truth, and the consequent pleasantness, are signified by the “twelve springs of waters,” for “springs” signify truths; the affection of truth from good, and the consequent delight, are signified by the “seventy palm-trees” (of which below).

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Exodus 15:27, moving from the "twelve springs of water" (representing abundant truths) to the "seventy palm-trees," which signify the various forms of spiritual good and the joy that follows a period of spiritual trial.</meta>

### EXODUS [N. 8369]

“palm-trees” signify goods <note>In this context, "goods" refers to the underlying intentions and qualities of the heart, rather than just physical items or good deeds.</note>; they also signify the affection for what is good and the resulting delight, for all true delight arises from the affection for good. Because this was the meaning of “palm-trees,” they were used in sacred celebrations, such as the Feast of Tabernacles, as described in the books of **Moses**:

> You shall take for yourselves on the first day the fruit of a tree of honor, branches of palm-trees, and a bough of a leafy tree, and willows of the brook; and you shall rejoice before Jehovah your God seven days (*Leviticus 23:40*);

By “the fruit of a tree of honor” is signified celestial good <note>The highest form of love, directed toward the Lord.</note>; by “palm-trees,” spiritual good, or the good of truth; by “a bough of a leafy tree,” <term>memory-knowledge</term> <note>original: "scientificum"—this refers to factual information stored in the memory which serves as a foundation for higher spiritual understanding.</note>; and by “willows of the brook,” the most basic truths of the <term>natural</term> <note>The "natural" refers to the external part of a person's life and mind that interacts with the physical world.</note>. Thus, these four items represent all categories of goods and truths in their proper order. 

[2] That “palm-trees” signified a holy celebration arising from what is good is also clear from these passages:

> A great crowd that had come to the feast, when they heard that Jesus was coming into Jerusalem, took branches of palm trees, and went out to meet Him, and cried out, Hosanna: Blessed is He that comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel (*John 12:12, 13*).

> I saw, and behold, a great crowd standing before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, and palms in their hands (*Revelation 7:9*).

> The vine has dried up, and the fig-tree withers; the pomegranate, and also the palm-tree; all joy has dried up from the sons of man (*Joel 1:12*).

> The righteous shall flourish like the palm-tree; he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon (*Psalm 92:12*);

In this instance, the “palm-tree” represents good, and the “cedar” represents truth. 

[3] Since a “palm-tree” signifies good, it also signifies wisdom, because true wisdom comes from what is good. This was represented by the palm-trees which, along with the <term>cherubim</term> <note>Symbolic celestial beings representing the Lord's providence and protection of the holy.</note> and flowers, were carved onto the walls of the Temple. “The Temple” signified the Lord Himself, and in a symbolic sense, heaven (see section numbers 2777, 3720). The “cherubim,” the “palm-trees,” and the “flowers upon the walls” signified Providence, wisdom, and intelligence, which come from the Lord—thus representing all things belonging to heaven. That these were carved on the walls of the temple is shown in the first book of **Kings**:

# [N. 8369] CHAPTER XV. VER. 27

Solomon carved all the walls of the house round about with openings of carvings of cherubs and palm-trees, and openings of flowers; and upon the two doors of <term>woods of oil</term> <note>original: "lignis olivi"—this refers to olive wood, which in the biblical context symbolizes the good of love and peace.</note> he carved carvings of cherubs and of palm-trees, and of openings of flowers, and overlaid them with gold, so that he overspread the gold upon the cherubs, and upon the palm-trees (*1 Kings 6:29, 32*);

By these carvings, the state of heaven was represented. By the "cherubs," the Providence of the Lord is signified, meaning that all things come from Him (that cherubs denote Providence, see n. 308). By "palm-trees," he represented wisdom, which comes from the <term>good</term> <note>In this spiritual philosophy, "good" is not just a moral category but the actual life-force of love flowing from the Divine.</note> of the Lord; and by "flowers," intelligence, which comes from the truth provided by Him. By the "gold" with which the cherubs and palm-trees were overlaid, was signified the good of love which reigns universally in the heavens. (That "gold" denotes the good of love, see n. 113, 1551, 1552, 5658.) Therefore, also, where the new temple is described in the book of **Ezekiel**—which signifies the Lord's heaven—it is said that cherubs and palm-trees were upon the walls everywhere (*Ezekiel 41:17, 18, 20, 25, 26*).

**8370.** *And they encamped there by the waters.* That this signifies that after <term>temptation</term> <note>Spiritual "temptation" here refers to a period of internal struggle or trial where a person's faith is tested.</note> the truths of faith were set in order by means of the good of love, is evident from the meaning of "encamping," which refers to the arrangement or organization of truth and good (n. 8103, 8130, 8131, 8155); and from the meaning of "waters," which refers to the truths of faith (n. 2702, 3058, 3424, 4976, 5668). 

The reason that "encamping there by the waters" signifies that the truths of faith were organized by the good of love is because a "camp" signifies truths and goods (n. 8193, 8196), and "encamping" signifies their systematic arrangement. Being "by the waters" signifies that this happens according to the truths which come from the <term>Divine</term> <note>The Divine refers to God, specifically as the source of all truth and love.</note>. It is said to be "by means of the good of love" because all organization of truths is carried out by love; for it is under the influence of love that truths find their place and join with that love to form, as it were, a single body. 

It is also said that this happens "according to the image of the man in whom they are." This is because the image of a person's spirit—which is the person's true self, the <term>inward man</term> <note>The "inward man" is the eternal, spiritual part of a person that lives on after the body dies.</note>—is formed precisely by how truths and goodness are organized within them. This is why, when angels are present, a "sphere" of love radiates from them and affects everyone nearby, and the truths of their faith shine forth from them.

### CONTINUATION CONCERNING THE SPIRITS AND INHABITANTS OF THE EARTH JUPITER.

**8371.** I have been further informed by the spirits who are from that earth about various things that concern its inhabitants, such as their walk, their food, their homes, and the like. As regards their walk, they do not walk erect like the inhabitants of this and of many other earths, nor do they creep in the manner of animals, but when they are walking they assist themselves with the palms of their hands, and alternately half raise themselves on their feet, and also at every third step turn the face to the side and behind them, and also at the same time bend the body a little, which is done rapidly. For among them it is unbecoming to be looked at by others except in the face.

**8372.** When they are walking in this way they always keep the face forward, and thus look before them; and never downward, or toward the earth. To look downward they call <term>damnable</term> <note>original: "damnabile"—this suggests that looking down is seen as a spiritual failure or a rejection of higher, heavenly things.</note>. Only the lowest among them do this, who, unless they accustom themselves to look forward, are banished from society.

**8373.** But when they sit, they appear like the men of our earth, erect as to the upper part of the body; but they sit with their feet crossed. They are extremely careful, not only when they walk, but also when they sit, not to be looked at from behind, but in the face. Moreover, they are very willing for their faces to be seen, because from this appears their <term>mind</term> <note>original: "animus"—referring to the inner disposition, intentions, or "soul" of the person as expressed through their features.</note>; for they never show a face at variance with their mind; this being impossible.

### N. 8373] SPIRITS AND INHABITANTS OF JUPITER

From this also those who are present know clearly what mind they have toward them, which they do not hide; and especially whether a seeming friendship is sincere, or pretended.

**8374.** These things have been shown me by their spirits, and have been confirmed by their angels. Consequently also their spirits are not seen walking erect like others; but almost like persons swimming in water, helping themselves forward with their hands, and by turns looking around them. <note>The author describes a spiritual representation of their character; their "swimming" motion suggests a life lived in a fluid state of natural goodness rather than the rigid, "upright" intellectualism of other spirits.</note>

**8375.** They who live in their warm zones go naked, but with a covering round the loins; nor are they ashamed of their nakedness, for their minds are <term>chaste</term> <note>In this context, "chastity" refers to a state of spiritual purity where sexual love is focused exclusively on one's spouse and is inseparable from divine love.</note>; and they love none except their <term>consorts</term> <note>A formal term for a husband or wife.</note>, and abhor adulteries. They were very much surprised that when the spirits of our earth saw them walking in this way, and likewise naked, they ridiculed them, and also had lascivious thoughts; and that they paid no attention whatever to their <term>celestial life</term> <note>A life characterized by the highest level of love for the Lord and the neighbor.</note>; but only to such things. They said that this is a sign that they care more for bodily and earthly things than for heavenly ones; and that indecencies possess their minds. They were told that nakedness does not cause either shame or scandal to those who live in chastity, and in a state of innocence; but only to those who live in lasciviousness and shamelessness.

**8376.** When the inhabitants of that earth are lying in bed, they turn their face forward, or into the chamber; but not backward, or to the wall. Their spirits told me this, and stated the reason: that they believe that in this way they turn their face to the Lord, but if backward, that they would turn it away. A similar thing had sometimes happened to me, when I was in bed, but I had not previously known the source of it. <note>In the author's theology, the "face" is the index of the interiors; to turn the face toward something is to align one's entire spiritual being with it.</note>

**8377.** They take delight in prolonged eating, not so much for the enjoyment of the food, as for that of conversation at that time. When they sit at table, they do not sit upon chairs or benches, nor upon raised couches of grass, nor upon the grassy turf; but upon the leaves of a certain tree. They were not willing to tell of what tree the leaves were, but when I mentioned several by guess, and at last mentioned the leaves of the **fig-tree**, they assented. <note>The fig-tree often symbolizes "natural good," or the practical, external expression of a good heart.</note>

They bestow great care in forming and cleaning these tents, and they also have their meals in them.

# CHAPTER THE SIXTEENTH.

### THE DOCTRINE OF CHARITY.

**8387.** He who wishes to be saved must confess his sins and do **repentance** <term>From the Latin *poenitentia*; a complete turning away from past wrongs and a change of life</term>.

**8388.** To confess sins is to become thoroughly acquainted with evils, to see them in one's self, to acknowledge them, to regard one's self as guilty, and to condemn one's self on account of them. When this is done before God, it is to confess sins.

<meta>This page transitions from the observations of the spirits of Jupiter to a systematic explanation of the "Doctrine of Charity." It focuses specifically on the nature of repentance and the difference between genuine spiritual change and mere verbal confession.</meta>

<page-num>191</page-num>
<header>N. 8389] THE DOCTRINE OF CHARITY</header>

**8389.** To practice **repentance** <term>The process of turning away from selfish behaviors to lead a life based on spiritual principles</term> is to desist from sins and to lead a new life according to the commands of faith, after one has confessed their sins and made a humble, heartfelt plea for forgiveness.

**8390.** A person who merely admits they are a sinner like everyone else, and views themselves as guilty of all evils without examining themselves—that is, without actually seeing their specific sins—may make a confession, but it is not the confession of repentance. This is because they continue to live afterward exactly as they did before.

**8391.** One who leads a life of faith practices repentance daily. Such a person reflects on the evils within themselves, acknowledges them, guards against them, and prays to the Lord for help. By their own nature, a human is constantly falling, but is continually being raised up by the Lord. A person "falls" from their own nature when they dwell on evil thoughts with desire; they are raised up by the Lord when they resist that evil and, as a result, do not act upon it. 

This is the state of all who are in **good** <term>A state of being where actions are motivated by love for others and God</term>. However, those who are in **evil** <term>A state of being motivated by self-interest and worldly desires</term> are also constantly falling and being uplifted by the Lord—but in their case, the Lord's uplifting is to prevent them from falling into the most severe **hell** <note>In this context, "hell" refers to a spiritual state of extreme selfishness and misery</note> possible, toward which they naturally incline with all their strength. In this way, the Lord actually uplifts them into a milder state of suffering.

**8392.** Repentance is effective when performed in a **state of freedom**; but when it is performed in a **state of compulsion**, it is not effective. 

->States of Compulsion<-
*   A state of sickness
*   A state of mental depression following misfortune
*   The proximity of death
*   Any state of fear that takes away the use of sound reason

When an evil person promises repentance or does good while in a state of compulsion, they return to their former life of evil as soon as they return to a state of freedom. It is different for a good person; for them, such states are times of **temptation** <term>Spiritual trials or internal conflicts where one's character is tested</term> in which they emerge victorious.

**8393.** Repentance of the mouth is not true repentance if it is not also a repentance of the life. Sins are not forgiven through verbal repentance, but through a change in how one lives. Sins are continually being forgiven by the Lord, for He is mercy itself; yet sins "stick" to a person no matter how much they believe they have been forgiven, and they are only removed through a life lived according to the commands of faith. So far as

as a person lives according to these commands, so far their sins are removed; and as far as they are removed, so far they have been forgiven. For man is withheld from evil and held in good by the Lord; and he is able to be withheld from evil in the afterlife to the same extent that he resisted evil during his life in the body. Furthermore, he can be held in what is good at 그that time to the same extent that he did what was good out of genuine affection during his life in the body. This demonstrates what the **forgiveness of sins** <term>In this context, forgiveness is not a one-time legal pardon, but a gradual process of being spiritually distanced from selfish impulses</term> is, and where it comes from. Anyone who believes that sins are forgiven in any other way is greatly mistaken.

**8394.** After a person has examined themselves, acknowledged their sins, and performed **repentance** <term>The act of turning away from past wrongs to start a new spiritual path</term>, they must remain constant in doing good until the end of their life. If, however, they later fall back into their former life of evil and embrace it, they commit **profanation** <note>original: "profanatio"; the act of mixing sacred truths with a lifestyle of evil, which causes a deeper spiritual conflict</note>, for they then join evil with good. Consequently, their later state becomes worse than their previous one, according to the Lord's words:

> When the unclean spirit goes out of a man, he walks through dry places, seeking rest, but finds none; then he says, "I will return into my house from which I came out"; and when he has come, and finds it empty, swept, and decorated for him, then he goes and joins to himself seven other spirits worse than himself, and having entered in they dwell there; and the last things of the man become worse than the first (*Matthew* 12:43–45).

16. This is the word that Jehovah <term>Jehovah: The sacred name for God in the Hebrew Bible, often used in this commentary to signify the Divine Being as the source of all love and life</term> hath commanded: "Gather of it, every one according to his appetite; an omer <term>omer: An ancient Hebrew unit of dry measure, approximately equal to two liters or two quarts</term> per head, according to the number of your souls; take ye every one for those who are in his tent."

17. And the sons of Israel did so, and they gathered, collecting some more and some less.

18. And when they measured it with the omer, the one who gathered much had nothing left over, and the one who gathered little had no lack; they gathered every one according to his eating <note>This verse emphasizes a spiritual principle: that Divine grace is received by everyone according to their individual capacity to receive it, ensuring no one is overwhelmed and no one is left wanting</note>.

19. And Moses said unto them, "Let no one leave a residue <note>residue: refers here to leftovers or hoarding for the next day</note> of it until the morning."

20. And they did not listen to Moses; for some men left a residue of it until the morning, and it bred worms and stank; and Moses was angry with them.

21. And they gathered it morning by morning, every one according to his appetite; and when the sun grew hot, it melted.

22. And it happened that on the sixth day they gathered twice as much bread, two omers for each one; and all the leaders of the community came and told Moses.

23. And he said unto them, "This is what Jehovah spoke: A rest, a holy sabbath <term>sabbath: From the Hebrew 'shabbat', meaning to cease; a day of rest signifying the union of the Divine and the human</term> to Jehovah, is tomorrow. Bake what you will bake, and boil what you will boil; and all that is left over, set aside for yourselves to keep until the morning."

24. And they set it aside until the morning, as Moses commanded, and it did not stink, and no worm was found in it.

25. And Moses said, "Eat this today, because today is a sabbath to Jehovah; today you shall not find it in the field.

26. Six days you shall gather it, and on the seventh day is the sabbath; it shall not be found on that day."

27. And it happened on the seventh day that some of the people went out to gather, and they found none.

28. And Jehovah said unto Moses, "How long do you refuse to keep My commandments and My laws?

29. See, because Jehovah hath given you the sabbath, therefore He giveth you on the sixth day the bread of two days; rest ye every one in his place; let no one go forth from his place on the seventh day."

30. And the people rested on the seventh day.

**35.** And the sons of Israel did eat the manna forty years, until they came to a land inhabited; they did eat the manna until they came unto the border of the land of Canaan <note>This signifies the period of spiritual preparation and instruction before entering a state of rest or a "heavenly" state</note>.

**36.** And an omer is the tenth part of an ephah <term>ephah: A larger Hebrew unit of dry measure; the tenth part suggests a specific spiritual proportion of goodness received</term>.

## THE CONTENTS.

**8395.** The preceding chapter treated of the second temptation of those who were of the spiritual church, which was from truth being perceived as undelightful. In this chapter, in the internal sense <term>internal sense: The deeper, spiritual meaning of the Scripture that lies beneath the literal historical narrative</term>, a third temptation is treated of, which is from the lack of good <note>In this context, "good" refers to the love and charity that nourish the soul, just as "truth" refers to the knowledge that guides it</note>. By the lack of bread and of flesh, at which the sons of Israel murmured, is signified a lack of good. Consolation after temptation is signified and described by the manna which they received, and by the quail. Manna denotes spiritual good. That this was given to them by the Lord continually, and without any care and aid of theirs, is signified by their receiving the manna daily, and by the worm breeding in it if they gathered more.

### THE INTERNAL SENSE.

**8396.** Verse 1. *And they journeyed from Elim, and all the assemblage of the sons of Israel came unto the wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai, in the fifteenth day of the second month of their going out of the land of Egypt.* "And they journeyed from Elim," signifies what is successive <note>Successive: Refers to the orderly progression of spiritual states, one following another</note>; "and all the assemblage of the sons of Israel came unto the wilderness of Sin," signifies unto another state of temptation; "which is between Elim and Sinai," signifies what is continuous and its quality; "in the fifteenth day of the second month," signifies the state relatively; "of their going out of the land of Egypt," signifies to their state when they were first liberated from infestations <term>infestations: In this context, the spiritual pressure or "attacks" from negative influences that clouded the mind while in a lower state (Egypt)</term>.

**8397.** *And they journeyed from Elim.* That this signifies what is successive, is evident from the signification of "journeying," as being what is successive and continuous (see n. 4375, 4554, 4585, 5996, 8181, 8345) <note>These numbers refer to other entries in the "Arcana Coelestia" where Swedenborg establishes these definitions</note>; and from the signification of "Elim," as being a state of consolation after temptation (n. 8367), consequently by "they journeyed from Elim," is signified what is successive of life in respect to states of temptations. For when those who are of the spiritual church <term>spiritual church: A term for people who are guided by intellectual truths and conscience rather than direct celestial perception</term> are undergoing temptations, they are brought from one temptation into another. This is the successive that is here signified by "journeying." That "journeying" signifies what is successive of life, is because there are no spaces, as there are no times, in the other life; but states instead of them (n. 2625, 2837, 3356, 3387, 4321, 4882, 5605, 7381). Consequently movements do not signify movements, nor journeyings, journeyings; but changes and successions of states.

**8398.** *And all the assemblage of the sons of Israel came unto the wilderness of Sin.* That this signifies unto another state of temptation, is evident from the signification of "coming," as being the abode of the successive that is signified by "journeying" (see n. 8397); from the signification of "the assemblage of the sons of Israel," as being those who are of the spiritual church (n. 7843); from the signification of "the wilderness," as being a state of undergoing temptations (see n. 8098); and...

**8398.** ...from the meaning of “Sin,” as representing the quality of this specific state; for names in the Word encompass the entire quality of the state of the subject being discussed, as has been shown many times before. From the temptation <note>temptation: In this context, a spiritual trial or crisis where one's faith and character are tested.</note> which is signified by the people’s grumbling because they lacked bread and meat, and from the comfort that followed—represented by the manna and the quail—it is clear what “Sin” signifies: namely, the good that comes from truth. Consequently, “Sin,” which was a city in Egypt and gave its name to the Wilderness of Sin, signifies in its opposite sense the evil that arises from false ideas. This is seen in the book of *Ezekiel*:

> I will pour out My wrath upon Sin, the strength of Egypt; and I will cut off the multitude of No; and I will set a fire in Egypt, grieving Sin shall grieve, and No shall be for a breaking through, and Noph for the enemies daily; the young men of Aven and of Pi-beseth shall fall by the sword, and these shall go into captivity; and in Tehaphnehes the day shall be darkened, when I shall break there the yokes of Egypt (**xxx 15-18**);

[2] In this passage, the text describes those who are in <term>memory-knowledges: The original Latin term is *scientifica*, referring to facts, information, and academic data stored in the external memory.</term> and who use that information to hatch false ideas which then lead to evils. Here, “Egypt” represents this factual knowledge; “Sin” represents the evil that springs from a false perspective; and “No” represents the false perspective itself that gives rise to evil. Anyone can see that a deeper, hidden meaning lies beneath the literal words here, simply by considering that the Word is Divine. Unless there were a deeper sense within it, there would be hardly any meaning that the mind could grasp, let alone a sense that contains anything holy. It is therefore very clear that the names in the Word represent actual things, and from these names, a general spiritual meaning emerges that is worthy of the Word which comes from Jehovah. Anyone who acknowledges the Word to be Divine cannot possibly deny this, provided they are willing to think rationally or draw conclusions from an understanding that is, even for a moment, enlightened by higher truth.

For “Elim,” with its fountains and palm trees, signifies the truth and goodness that provide comfort after a spiritual trial (as seen in the final verse of the previous chapter); and “Sinai”...

The "good that is from truth" is the good found in the spiritual person before <term>regeneration: The process of spiritual rebirth where a person's internal priorities shift from selfish desires to heavenly love.</term> for at that stage, they do good because it is truth—that is, because it has been commanded, and therefore out of obedience. **8400.** *On the fifteenth day of the second month.* That this signifies the state relatively, is evident from the meaning of the number "fifteen," from the meaning of "day," and from the meaning of "month." By "month" is signified the end of a former state and the beginning of the following state, thus a new state; by "day" is signified state in general; and by "fifteenth" is signified what is new. This is because "fourteen days," or "two weeks," signifies an entire period or a state from its beginning to its end; consequently, "fifteen" signifies what is new—in this case, a new stage of life. This new life is represented by the manna they received from heaven; for "manna" denotes the "good of truth," which is the very life of the spiritual person. The number "fifteen" carries a similar meaning to the number "eight," because the eighth day is the first day of the following week. <note>In biblical symbolism, the number eight often represents a new beginning, such as the first day after a completed cycle of seven.</note>

**8401.** *Of their going out of the land of Egypt.* That this signifies their state when they were first liberated from <term>infestations: In this context, spiritual "infestations" refer to the persistent pressure and mental disturbances caused by negative influences or false ideas.</term> is evident from the meaning of "going out" and "being brought out," which refers to being liberated; and from the meaning of "the land of Egypt," which refers to infestations by those who are in evil and the resulting false ideas.

### N. 8408] CHAPTER XVI. VERSES 2, 3

...the good and truth of the church. Doctrine is signified by “the pot” in which, by the command of Elisha, pottage was boiled for the sons of the prophets, as we read in the second book of *Kings*:

> Elisha returned to Gilgal when there was a famine in the land, and the sons of the prophets were sitting before him. He said to his servant, “Set on the large pot, and boil pottage for the sons of the prophets.” One went out into the field to gather vegetables, and found a wild vine of the field, and gathered from it wild gourds, and sliced them into the pot of pottage. While they were eating the pottage, they cried out, “Death in the pot, O man of God!” But he said they should take meal <note>Original: *farina*; likely a fine flour or meal used here as a symbol of spiritual truth.</note>, which he threw into the pot; and he said, “Pour out for the people, and let them eat.” Then there was no evil thing in the pot (iv. 38–41);

Be it known that all Divine miracles involve things belonging to the Lord’s kingdom and church (n. 7337, 8364). Here, Elisha represents the Word of the Lord (n. 2762), and the prophets represent the doctrines derived from it (n. 2534, 7269). From this, it is clear what aspect of the church was represented by this miracle: specifically, that the good of the church which has been falsified <note>Falsification refers to taking a spiritual truth and twisting its meaning to serve a selfish or incorrect purpose.</note> becomes good again by means of truth from the Word. In this story, “famine” denotes a lack of knowledge regarding truth and good; “the pot” signifies doctrine; “pottage” signifies the good of the external rituals of the Jewish church; “wild gourds from the vine of the field” represent falsification; and “meal” represents truth from the Word (n. 2177). Through this truth, that which has been falsified—described as “death in the pot”—is transformed into something good. The reason “pots” signify containers of good is that they were useful vessels in which food was prepared; and since food of all kinds signifies things that nourish the soul (such as the affections for good and truth), the vessels that hold them represent the doctrines containing those affections (n. 681, 1480, 3114, 4792, 5147, 5293, 5340, 5342, 5576, 5915).

**8409.** As “flesh” signifies one’s own <term>Latin: *proprium*; this refers to a person's "selfhood" or inherent nature—what they are when left to themselves</term> in both senses: in the highest sense, it signifies the Lord’s Divine Own (His Divine Human), and thus the good of His love toward the entire human race; therefore, when "flesh" refers to a human being, it denotes one's own nature made alive by the Lord—the Lord’s presence within a person, or the good of love directed toward Him (see n. 3813, 7850).

But in the opposite sense, “flesh” denotes man’s own <term>selfhood</term> apart from the Divine, meaning the evil of self-love, and the cravings or lusts <note>Original: *concupiscentiae*; strong desires or "concupiscences" that drive a person toward selfish ends.</note> arising from that love (n. 999, 3813). That "flesh" can also denote those in whom good and truth have been destroyed, see n. 4503.

[2] Again:

> Utter a parable against the house of rebellion, and say unto them, Thus said the Lord *Jehovih* <note>Original: *Jehovih*; Swedenborg uses this specific Hebrew-derived name to distinguish the Lord’s power in relation to both good and truth</note>: “Set on the pot, set it on, and also pour the pieces into it, every good piece, the thigh, and the shoulder; fill it with the choice of the bones.” Said the Lord *Jehovih*: “Woe to the city of bloods, to the pot whose scum is therein, and whose scum is not gone out of it!” (*Ezekiel* xxiv. 3, 4, 6);

Here “the pot” denotes a city, or the people within it, who are characterized by the evil of the profanation of good <note>Profanation refers to the act of knowing what is good or true and then deliberately living a life contrary to it, which "scums" or defiles the spiritual state.</note>. The good which is “the flesh” in this passage refers to “the thigh and the shoulder,” while the evil is “the scum” rising from them. The profanation of good is the “scum” that remains; therefore, it is also called “the city of bloods.”

[3] In *Jeremiah*:

> *Jehovah* said unto *Jeremiah*, “What seest thou?” I said, “I see a pot that is boiling, whose face is toward the north.” Then *Jehovah* said, “From the north evil shall be opened upon all the inhabitants of the land” (i. 12–14);

Here a “boiling pot” denotes a people who have been taken over by falsities. “The north” denotes the sensuous and...

<meta>This page continues the spiritual interpretation of Exodus chapter 16, moving from the symbolism of the "pot" (doctrine) to a detailed analysis of "flesh." It establishes that in the internal sense of the Word, "flesh" represents the human "self" or "ego" (proprium), which is inherently inclined toward evil and lacks spiritual life unless animated by the Divine Spirit.</meta>

### [N. 8409] EXODUS

Man’s own <note>The original Latin term is *proprium*, referring to the "selfhood" or the part of a person that feels like it belongs only to them, which Swedenborg describes as being naturally focused on selfish desires.</note> is nothing but evil (see references n. 210, 215, 694, 874–876, 987, 1023, 1044, 1047, 3812, 5660, 5786). That “flesh” signifies man’s own—and thus evil of every kind—is further evident from the following passages in the Book of *Isaiah*:

> I will feed your oppressors with their own flesh, and they shall be drunken with their own blood, as with new wine (xlix. 26);

“To feed with flesh” signifies being gorged with one’s own evil. 

[2] In the Book of *Jeremiah*:

> Cursed is the man that trusts in man, and makes flesh his arm, but his heart departs from Jehovah (xvii. 5);

“To make flesh his arm” signifies to trust in one’s own power; and therefore in *Isaiah* ix. 20 “to eat the flesh of his arm” signifies to trust in oneself. Again in *Isaiah*:

> Egypt is a man, and not God; and his horses are flesh, and not spirit (xxxi. 3);

“The horses of Egypt” signify <term>memory-knowledges</term> <note>Original: *scientifica*. These are external facts or information stored in the memory, which can be used to justify wrong ideas if the person's understanding is perverted.</note> from a perverted understanding (n. 6125). “Flesh” signifies what is dead; “spirit” signifies what is alive; therefore the sons of Egypt are said to be “great in flesh” (*Ezekiel* xvi. 26). What is “dead” is so called from evil, for spiritual death comes from evil; and what is “alive” is so called from good, for spiritual life comes from good. 

[3] Because of this, “flesh” and “spirit” in the Word are opposed to each other, as in the following passages:

> That which is born from the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the spirit is spirit (*John* iii. 6).

> It is the spirit that makes alive, the flesh profits nothing; the words that I speak to you are spirit, and are life (*John* vi. 63).

> Jehovah said, My Spirit shall not reprove man forever, for he is indeed flesh (*Genesis* vi. 3);

Here “flesh” signifies man’s own self. In the same way in the following:

> Jesus said, Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed it, but My Father who is in the heavens (*Matthew* xvi. 17).

> As many as received Him, to them He gave power to be sons of God, to them that believe on His name; who were born, not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God (*John* i. 12, 13);

“The will of the flesh” signifies the "selfhood" of the will; “the will of man” signifies the "selfhood" of the understanding; “sons of God” signify those who are reborn into spiritual life.

<summary>This page explains the biblical symbolism of "flesh" as representing the human ego or self-will (proprium), contrasting it with "spirit" as the source of true spiritual life. It provides a linguistic and theological cross-reference to show that "flesh" throughout the Bible often refers to self-reliance and inherent evil rather than physical skin.</summary>

# [N. 8409] CHAPTER XVI. VERSES 2, 3

Those who are reborn—and those in the process of being reborn—are all given life from the Lord’s own nature, which is called “the flesh and body of the Lord,” and is actually Divine Goodness itself. [4] However, when “flesh” is used in the opposite sense, it refers to a person’s own selfish nature, and thus to evil. In this sense, it also signifies <term>concupiscence</term> <note>This term refers to intense, often misdirected, worldly or physical desires that distract from spiritual growth.</note>, because the life of the flesh (the body’s own life) is nothing more than the pleasure of the senses, the satisfaction of appetites, and lust. That “flesh” signifies this kind of selfish craving is clear from these words in the books of *Moses*:

> The rabble that was in the midst of the people felt a great longing, which caused the sons of Israel to weep again and say, "Who shall feed us with flesh? Our soul is now dry, and our eyes have nothing to look at but this manna." And Jehovah said to Moses, "Say to the people: Sanctify yourselves for tomorrow, so that you may eat flesh, for you have wept in the ears of Jehovah, saying, 'Who shall feed us with flesh? For it was better with us in Egypt.' Jehovah will give you flesh to eat for a whole month, until it comes out of your nose and becomes loathsome to you." The flesh was still between their teeth, before it was even swallowed, when the anger of Jehovah was kindled against the people; and Jehovah struck the people with a very great plague. Therefore, he called the name of that place “the graves of lust,” because there they buried the people who had lusted (*Numbers xi. 4, 6, 16, 18, 20, 33, 34*).

From all of this, it is now clear what is meant by “sitting by the flesh-pot in the land of Egypt.” It signifies a life lived according to one’s own whims and cravings—a life centered entirely on the self.

**8410.** *When we did eat bread to satiety.* That this signifies that they had enjoyed the pleasures of the world as much as they wished, is evident from the meaning of “eating,” which signifies taking something into oneself and making it one’s own (see references n. 3168, 3513, 3596, 4745), and also enjoyment (n. 7849). It is also evident from the meaning of “bread.” In a positive sense, bread represents the good of a heavenly life; however, in the opposite sense, it represents the "good" of a natural life that is cut off from heaven—in other words, the "good" of selfish pleasures. 

In a spiritual sense, “bread” refers to the primary thing that nourishes the soul and keeps its spiritual life alive. For those in heaven, this is the good of love, which is the very essence of heavenly life. But in the opposite sense, “bread” refers to the primary thing that nourishes those in hell and sustains their existence. For them, this is the evil of self-love and love of the world. To them, this evil *is* "good," because nothing feels more delightful or sweet to them than following their own selfish desires.

<summary>This page explains that "flesh" can represent either Divine Goodness or selfish lust, and identifies "bread" as the essential nourishment of the soul, whether that nourishment be heavenly love or hellish self-interest.</summary>

### EXODUS [N. 8410]

This is what is meant here by “the good of pleasures.” Based on the meaning of “to satiety,” this refers to having as much as they desired; for with those who are good, the will is satisfied with what is good, while with those who are evil, the will is satisfied with what is evil.

**8411.** *For you have brought us forth.* This signifies the state after they were set free. In this context, "bringing forth" from the land of Egypt represents being liberated from a state of <term>infestations</term> <note>In this spiritual context, "infestations" refers to being harassed or overwhelmed by negative thoughts and external spiritual pressures that cloud the mind.</note>.

**8412.** *Into this wilderness.* This signifies a state of <term>temptations</term> <note>These are not merely physical hardships, but inner spiritual struggles where a person's character and faith are tested.</note>, as is evident from the symbolic meaning of a “wilderness” (see section 8098).

**8413.** *To kill this whole community with hunger.* This signifies that they felt they were dying from a lack of joy and goodness. "To kill" means to take away life—specifically the life that comes from delight and goodness, which is what human life truly consists of (see sections 3607, 6767). The “community” refers to those who belong to the spiritual church (see section 7843). “Hunger” refers to a lack of goodness (see section 5893)—specifically the "good of pleasures" symbolized by “bread.” When the nourishment of the spirit is taken away, a spiritual hunger follows.

[2] Here is how this process works: When the "good of charity"—which forms the spiritual life—is being introduced into a person, the old delights of worldly pleasures are removed. When these old joys are taken away, the person enters into a state of trial or <term>temptation</term>. They believe that if they are deprived of these pleasures, they are deprived of all life, because their natural life was built on those delights (or what they called "good"). They do not yet realize that when this lower delight is removed, a higher spiritual delight or "good" is given by the Lord in its place. This higher good is symbolized by the “manna.” The former pleasures are meant by the “flesh and bread in the land of Egypt,” and the loss of those pleasures is meant by “hunger.”

[3] However, it should be carefully noted that a person who is undergoing <term>regeneration</term> <note>The process of spiritual rebirth or being made "new" by aligning one's life with Divine goodness.</note> is not actually deprived of the pleasures of the body and the mind. In fact, they enjoy these pleasures even more fully after their transformation than they did before—but the priority changes. Before <term>regeneration</term>, these worldly pleasures were the primary focus of their life; but afterward...

<summary>This page explains that "hunger" in the desert symbolizes a spiritual crisis where old worldly pleasures are removed to make room for higher, spiritual joys (symbolized by manna). It clarifies that spiritual growth does not destroy the capacity for pleasure, but reorders it so that divine goodness becomes the primary source of life.</summary>

### CHAPTER XVI. VERSES 4, 5

than the <term>influx</term><note>A central concept in this work, referring to the way spiritual energy and thought "flow" from the spiritual world into the human mind.</note> of the spiritual world into the ideas of thought, and thus into words; for without this influx who would ever say “walking” to express living? as “walking in the law,” “in the statutes,” “in the commandments,” or “in the fear of God.” The case is very similar with “going,” as denoting to live (of which see above, n. 8417), and also with “journeying,” “advancing,” and “sojourning.” That these expressions denote living is because in the spiritual world there are no physical spaces, but instead there are <term>states of life</term><note>The author explains that in the afterlife, "distance" is not measured in miles, but by the difference or similarity in a person's inner character or mood.</note> (see n. 2625, 2684, 2837, 3356, 3387, 4321, 4882, 5605, 7381).

**8421.** *And it shall be in the sixth day.* That this signifies in the end of every state, is evident from the signification of “day,” as being a state (see n. 23, 487, 488, 493, 2788, 3462, 3785, 4850, 7680); and from the signification of “the sixth,” as being the end of a state. The gathering of the manna every day signifies the reception of good, and the eating of it signifies appropriation; consequently, “to prepare that which they have brought” signifies the arrangement or disposal of the goods which have been made part of one's life. This disposal is effected by the Lord at the end of every state, which is signified by “the sixth.” Conjunction follows this disposal, and this conjunction is signified by “the seventh day.”

**8423.** *And there shall be double over what they gather day by day.* That this signifies that the goods are to be conjoined, is evident from the signification of “there being double,” as being to be conjoined (that to be conjoined is signified by “double” is because the number “two” denotes conjunction, see n. 1686, 3519, 5194);
